sources.entry: Translation Caching: Skip, Don't Walk (the Page Table) - Defines the page-walk cache design space and shows why cached partial translations let a walk skip page-table levels.

summary.title: Translation Caching: Skip, Don't Walk (the Page Table)
summary.one_liner: Learn how MMU caches holding partial translations let x86-64 page-table walks skip upper levels of the radix tree after a TLB miss, and how five cache designs compare.
takeaways: Upper-level page table entries have strong temporal locality, so caching them in MMU-private caches avoids repeated memory accesses during TLB-miss walks.
Page table caches are tagged by physical address (like a data cache), while translation caches are tagged by virtual address indices (like a TLB) and can skip levels of the walk.
The paper defines five MMU cache organizations, including three new designs, and compares them quantitatively; translation cache variants perform best in many cases.
Radix tables with MMU caching cause far fewer DRAM accesses than inverted (hash-based) page tables, challenging earlier conclusions that hashing was better.
summary.summary: The paper (ISCA 2010, Barr, Cox, and Rixner) explores the design space of MMU caches that speed up page table walks after TLB misses in radix-tree page table architectures such as x86-64. It explains x86-64 address decomposition into four 9-bit indices and walks through how cached upper-level entries can be tagged by physical address (page table caches) or by virtual address indices (translation caches). It describes existing AMD Page Walk Cache and Intel Paging-Structure Caches alongside three new structures, then compares all five quantitatively in simulation. It also compares radix tables with MMU caches against inverted and hash-based page tables.
